description: Predominantly contrast gain. Two near-coincident solid CRFs on the left normalized-response axis: attended is shifted LEFT of ignored (a contrast-gain shift, visible separation ~0.05-0.10 in the mid-contrast rise) and both converge to a SHARED sub-1.0 plateau at ~0.61-0.62. Dashed percent-attentional-modulation curve on the right axis (0-100), largest (~98%) at low contrast and falling monotonically to ~0 by mid contrast. Shared scale with 2B (do NOT renormalize to 1.0).

provenance.figure_type: line/curve CRF, log-x; twin-y (left 0-1 normalized response, right 0-100 attentional modulation %)
provenance.tool_rationale: Mode-1 quantitative CRF plot: two solid sigmoids on the left axis plus one dashed % curve on the right axis. detect_plot_box gave a frame hint; final calibration is tick/frame-anchored from pixel-measured axis lines (see calibration). overlay + crop_region used for the adversarial alignment check.

calibration.anchor_method: Axis lines measured by longest-consecutive-dark-run per column/row on panel_A.jpg. Left y-axis = cols 33-34 (rows 40-332); right y-axis = cols 250-251 (rows 41-333); bottom x-axis = row 331-333. Tick labels verified by crop: left '1'/'0' and right '100'/'0' sit at the top/bottom frame corners respectively. x has NO numeric ticks on the paper (stimulus glyphs only), so x anchors are the frame edges set to the swept range [0.01, 1.0] per panel_A.md.
calibration.right_axis_render_note: overlay() takes one calibration; the right-axis percent_modulation curve (0-100) is rendered by passing value/100 through the left 0-1 calibration. Left and right axis pixel rows coincide (332<->40 vs 333<->41), so this lands the dashed curve on the right-axis ink to within ~1px.

per_curve.attended: solid CRF, traced; left/upper of unattended in the mid-contrast rise (contrast-gain shift). Spot-checked: x=0.1,y=0.5 -> row ~186 matches paper ink rows 187-190.
per_curve.unattended: solid CRF, traced; right/lower of attended. Spot-checked: x=0.1,y=0.41 -> row ~212 matches paper ink rows 213-217. Shared plateau ~0.615 -> row ~152 matches paper ink rows 151-154 at high contrast.
per_curve.percent_modulation: dashed right-axis curve, traced; 100 at low contrast falling monotonically to ~0. Rendered value/100 on the left calibration to hit the right axis.

provenance.normalization: Paper shared sub-1.0 scale (shared with 2B): solid CRFs converge to ~0.615, NOT pinned to 1.0. Confirmed against paper ink at high contrast.
caveats: x has no numeric ticks on the paper; x_range [0.01, 1.0] is taken from the frame edges per panel_A.md, not from labelled ticks.

DATA was confirmed faithful by pixel spot-checks (plateau, mid-rise of both CRFs); only the overlay's pixel mapping was wrong before this pass. The previous overlay used an approximate frame-edge calibration with no provenance block, producing a whole-curve shift. This pass re-rendered with the tick/frame-anchored calibration above.
percent_modulation dashed ink is broken/thick; its read values carry ~+/-3% uncertainty (e.g. x=0.1 reads ~19-23%).
provenance.re_digitization_2026_06_04: X-AXIS RE-LABELED to the AUTHOR contrast window [1e-5, 1] (paper/code/attentionModel/Figure2A.m cRange=[1e-5 1]; CODE-013/014/015/018). The paper panel has NO numeric x ticks, so the prior pass guessed the left frame edge at 0.01 (2 decades); the authors' script axis floor is 1e-5. The CURVE INK on the paper is unchanged - this is a pure x-axis frame RELABEL: each traced point keeps its exact pixel position, its contrast value is recomputed from the SAME log-fractional position across the frame under the author window (c_new = lo*(hi/lo)^f, f = the point's fractional log-x position in the old frame). The calibration.x pixel-col anchors were relabeled likewise. The overlay_*.png (ink-on-paper) is therefore still pixel-faithful; only the x-axis tick labels move. Resolution authority: author code (Phase-A resolver ladder rung 1). This closes the PAPER_ISSUE digitized-window tripwire (test_audit_2026_06_04_supplement.py) and makes the half-max / left-shift claims testable in-window.
